messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam, at twenty-one, had believed that coming home would be the end of it. The six months since his discharge, however, had proven to be a different kind of war. The convoy attack in Kandahar province was an event he carried not as a coherent story, but as a series of punishing sensory fragments. There was the deafening bang of the IED, a sound that seemed to tear the air itself, followed by the high-pitched whine that replaced all other noise. Then came the thick, acrid smell of burning diesel and rubber, a smell that clung to the back of his throat. He remembered the frantic shouting, the dust, and the rhythmic, gut-thumping sound of the medevac helicopter blades beating the air above them. These were the only pieces he had, and they offered no beginning or end.

Back in the US and driving a city bus, Liam found these pieces were not memories to be recalled but events to be relived. They played in his mind like a film on a loop, raw and immediate. The constant replay of these terrifying moments had solidified into a core belief: the world is a dangerous place. Because the trauma felt like it was still happening, he was certain that he had to be on guard all the time, that another attack could come at any moment, from any direction. This pervasive sense of threat coloured the memories themselves; when he scanned the faces of passengers getting on his bus, his hypervigilance would latch onto any perceived anomaly, and the fragmented images of the attack would surge forward, confirming his belief that danger was everywhere.

This conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe dictated the shrinking shape of his life. Crowds became unbearable gauntlets of potential threats, turning a simple trip to the shopping centre into an exercise in high-stakes threat assessment. He began to refuse invitations from friends, making excuses to avoid concerts or sporting events. Even the church his family attended felt like a liability, a soft target he couldn't bear to enter. His belief that he was in constant danger led him to systematically dismantle his social world, retreating into the perceived safety of isolation.

The intrusive memories were the most direct and powerful engine of this retreat. A truck backfiring on his route would instantly trigger the sound of the explosion, and for a few terrifying seconds, he was back in the dust and chaos. The smell of hot brakes from another vehicle could evoke the burning wreckage with such intensity that he would feel a wave of nausea. These moments were so distressing that his life became organized around preventing them and escaping them when they occurred. The moment his shift ended, he would return to his small apartment, draw the blinds, and lose himself for hours in the digital world of his phone or video games. It was a deliberate strategy of distraction; he had learned that if he kept his mind occupied with the screen, he could sometimes keep the film from playing in his head.

This very strategy of escape, however, kept the trauma alive. By spending every evening in a state of digital avoidance, he never allowed his mind the quiet space needed to process the event, to connect the fragmented pieces, or to file it away as something that was truly in the past. The memories remained stuck, potent, and terrifyingly current, ensuring they would be just as intrusive the next day. His avoidance prevented any new, corrective experiences that might challenge his belief that the world was dangerous. The less he engaged with the world, the more the traumatic memory defined it.

It was the sheer, grinding exhaustion of this cycle that finally brought him to therapy. His world had shrunk to the driver's seat of his bus and the glow of his monitor. The isolation had become a heavy blanket, and underneath it, a terrifying thought had begun to take root: he wasn't sure his life was worth living anymore. He struggled to find the words to explain the full experience, the story still a collection of disconnected pieces he couldn't assemble. He spoke instead of being haunted, of being trapped inside a film he couldn't turn off, hoping that someone could finally help him find the stop button.
